full_judgment: 28. Shahabuddin, J, who delivered the judgment of the Bench deciding the case of The Hanover Fire insurance Company has observed at page 138 of the Report that from the letter of the Deputy High. Commissioner for India in Pakistan, Dacca, dated the 27th September, 1950 it is clear that what had been agreed to by the two Governments was that the cases of the kind under consideration should be governed by Order XXVI of the Civil Procedure Code, and again at page 139 of the Report a similar observation has been made to the effect that the Governments of Pakistan and India are agreed that Order XXVI should govern the procedure in such cases. We do not know what better reciprocal arrangements could have been made than the said agreement indicating willingness of the Government of India to respect an order of a Pakistani Court issuing a commission for examination of a witness in India, made under the provision of Order XXVI, Rule 5 of the Code. Of course, what they agreed to was the law of their country and they could not but agree to it and similar was the case with Pakistan. We have already indicated that the provisions of section 78 and Order 26, rule 17 as are in force in India invest a commissioner appointed by a Court in Pakistan or Bangladesh with all necessary powers to execute the commission and vice versa and the agreement between the two Governments, as has been noticed in the said judgment, was also to the same effect. The learned Judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, however, seems to have been of the view that the import of the said agreement was not only that rule 5 of Order 26 should have application, but all the Rules of the said Order including rule 19 which deals with commissions issued at the instance of foreign tribunals should be applied. There should not be any shred of doubt that such is the case. Rule 19 of the said Order, as is in force in India, can certainly be invoked for examination of a witness in India, but that does not exclude the operation of rule 5, as is in force in Pakistan, and Rule 17 of the Order as is in force in India. By accepting that the matter relating to examination of a witness in India at the instance of a Court in Pakistan should be governed by the provisions of Order 26, the Government of India does not appear to have accepted the application of only rule 19 of that Order to the exclusion of the other Rules of the Order and, with great respect, we may say that we are unable to take such a limited view of the said agreement. We have no manner of doubt that if any additional agreement for reciprocal arrange rent, apart from the provisions of the local laws as were in force in the respective countries, was needed, the agreement of the Indian Government as contained in the letter of its Deputy High Commissioner at Dacca, was precisely the said kind of agreement, as was rightly held by the learned Judges of the Dacca High Court in their order refusing leave to appeal against the Judgment reported in 8 D.L.R. 186.
